<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par154 />{{GHGpar-heading|154|Sentences connected by Wāw}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|154|a}}
{{GHGterm|Wāw copulativum}}<ref>For further particulars of the use of {{GHGterm|wāw copulativum}}, see Gesenius’ ''Thesaurus'', i. 393 ff. On its use in the co-ordination of similar tenses and moods (e.g. five imperfects consecutive in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=25|verse=34}}, five perfects with {{GHGheb|text=וְגַם}}) as well as of dissimilar tenses and moods, the remarks made in the treatment of the tenses will suffice. With regard to the connexion of single ''nouns'' by {{GHGheb|text=וְ}} (which strictly speaking is always really a contraction of so many clauses into a single sentence) the following observations may be made:—<br><br>(''a'') Contrary to English usage, which in lengthy enumerations uses the ''and'' to connect only the last member of the series, in Hebrew ''polysyndeton'' is customary, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=12|verse=16}} wāw copulativum six times, 24:35 seven times, 15:19 ff. nine times, and in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=7|verse=24}} ten times. Sometimes, however, only the last two words are joined (so in a series of three members, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=5|verse=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=10|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=11|verse=26|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=14|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=39|hidebook=1}}, &c.; the last three out of a series of four, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=26}}); less frequently only the first two, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=45|verse=9}}; cf. {{GHGpar|132|d}}. The formula {{GHGheb|text=תְּמוֹל שִׁלְשׁוֹם|translate=yesterday}} (and) ''the day before yesterday'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=5|verse=8}}, &c., is always without the copula. On the other hand, the ''constructio asyndetos'' in a series of verbs is used as a rhetorical expedient to produce a hurried and so an impassioned description; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=5|verse=27}} ''at her feet he bowed, he fell, he lay''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=15|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=15}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=4|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=5|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=10|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=14|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=45|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=20|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=28|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=29|verse=8|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=2|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=5|verse=6|hidebook=1}}, &c.<br><br>(''b'') Frequently {{GHGterm|wāw copulativum}} is also ''explanatory'' (like ''isque, et—quidem'', and the German ''und zwar'', English ''to wit''), and is then called {{GHGterm|wāw explicativum}}, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=4}} and (i.e. ''namely'') ''of the fat thereof'' (unless it is simply copulative); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=24|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=25|verse=12|hidebook=1}} (''to wit two''); 27:14, 28:23, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=17|verse=3}} (in {{GHGheb|text=וּמַסֵּכָה}}; here as often elsewhere, to introduce an explanatory gloss, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=17|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=3|verse=15}}, and especially P. Haupt, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|SBOT.|Sacred Books of the Old Testament, ed. by P. Haupt. Lpz. and Baltimore, 1893 ff.}}}} Isaiah, p. 90, l. 21 ff.), {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=34}} ''and that too with the bear''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=57|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=17|verse=10}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=3|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=4|verse=10|hidebook=1}}, Ze 9:9, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=3|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=8|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=23|verse=10}} (but in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=28|verse=3}} the {{GHGheb|text=וּ}} before {{GHGheb|text=בְּעִירוֹ}} is to be omitted with the LXX); cf. also such combinations as {{GHGheb|text=וְעַד}}—{{GHGheb|text=מִן|translate=from... and even to...}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=14|verse=23|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=4|hidebook=1}}, 11, &c.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=6|verse=11}} (see Driver on the passage), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=1|verse=23}}, &c., {{GHGheb|text=ו}} is equivalent to ''yea, and''; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=32|verse=7}} ''even''.<br><br>{{GHGheb|text=וְ}} is used to express emphasis (=''and especially''), e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=16}} {{GHGheb|text=וְהֵֽרֹנֵךְ}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=2|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=18|verse=1}}, perhaps also in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=10|verse=17}} ''yea'', a whole ''host''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=16|verse=14}}.—An undoubted example of what is called {{GHGterm|wāw concomitantiae}} occurs in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=41|verse=12}} ''a seething pot'' {{GHGheb|text=וְאַגְמֹן|translate=with}} burning ''rushes''; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=10|verse=10}} (''with your little ones''), 12:8, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=1|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=42|verse=5}}. In Arabic this {{GHGterm|wāw concom.}} is followed by the accusative.<br><br>{{GHGheb|text=וְ-וְ}} is used in the sense of ''both''—''and'' in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=76|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=1|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=8|verse=13|hidebook=1}}. On {{GHGheb|text=וְ-וְ}} as meaning ''sive''—''sive'', cf. {{GHGpar|162|b}}.<br><br>(''c'') See the Lexicon on adverbs used in a copulative sense, such as {{GHGheb|text=גַּם|translate=also, moreover}}, summing up a number, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=גַּם־שְׁנַ֫יִם|translate=both together}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=27|verse=45}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=17|verse=15}}; {{GHGheb|text=גַּם־כֹּל|translate=all together}}; as an intensive ''and'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=30|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=37|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=30|verse=8}}; cf. also such examples as {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=24|verse=12}} ''see, yea see!'' {{GHGheb|text=גַּם-גַּם}} or {{GHGheb|text=גַּם-וְגַם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=44}}=''both''—''and''; {{GHGheb|text=גַּם}} occurs three times in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=24|verse=25}} and 32:20; also {{GHGheb|text=אַף}}, which is generally still more intensive, in the sense of ''also, in addition to this, even'', and belongs rather to poetry, and to the later language; frequently also equivalent to a mere ''and'', but sometimes adversative ''but now'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=44|verse=10}}, &c.; and {{GHGheb|text=אַף-אַף}} (also three times), equivalent to ''both—and''; cf. {{GHGheb|text=וְאַף גַּם|translate=and even}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=26|verse=44}}; {{GHGheb|text=אַף־כִּי}} prop. ''add to this also that'', equivalent to ''not to mention'', according to the context either ''quanto magis'' or ''quanto minus''.</ref> ({{GHGheb|text=וְ}}) serves to connect two or more sentences, or single words (on its various vocalization, cf. {{GHGpar|104|d}}–g). Its use, however, is by no means restricted merely to joining sentences which<section end=par154 /><noinclude>
